reading.title: Voices in the Canyon Wall
reading.purpose: Hike a red-rock canyon with a geologist to see how slow Earth forces leave clues in stone.
paras: Maya tightened her pack straps and looked up at the striped cliffs of Red Cedar Canyon. Her aunt Elena, a field geologist, tapped a crumbly orange band near the trail. "Millions of years ago, a slow river used to deposit fine sediment here, laying down sand and mud whenever the water slowed."

"How did loose mud turn into a wall this tall?" Maya asked. Aunt Elena pointed upward. "New layers kept arriving, so sand and silt began to accumulate, piling up hundreds of feet thick. The weight created steady pressure that squeezed water out and glued the grains into solid sandstone."

A few yards farther, Maya spotted a ridged fan shape pressed into gray stone. "Is that a fossil?" she whispered. Elena beamed. "Yes—the preserved print of an ancient seashell." She smiled at Maya. "That proves this dry desert once sat beneath a shallow sea."

Around the next bend, a dark stripe cut straight through the orange bands. "That band was once molten rock, melted deep underground by intense heat," Elena explained. "It pushed upward through a crack and cooled into hard black stone."

Finally, Elena traced a jagged line where the red stripes no longer lined up. "Here is a fault, a deep break in Earth's crust where huge blocks of rock shifted past each other. Far away, giant tectonic plates slowly collide along a boundary where two pieces of Earth's shell meet, bending and cracking rock across whole regions." Maya touched the cool stone, amazed that quiet cliffs told such a restless story.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "accumulate" most nearly means
choices: to melt into a hot liquid deep underground
to pile up gradually over a long period of time
to wash away quickly during a desert rainstorm
to split apart along a jagged crack in the cliff
qs.why: Paragraph 2 explains accumulate right after the comma as "piling up hundreds of feet thick."

qs.q: Which sentence shows what the seashell print tells Elena about the canyon's past?
choices: Maya tightened her pack straps and looked up at the striped cliffs of Red Cedar Canyon.
A few yards farther, Maya spotted a ridged fan shape pressed into gray stone.
"That proves this dry desert once sat beneath a shallow sea."
Around the next bend, a dark stripe cut straight through the orange bands.
qs.why: This sentence explains the conclusion Elena draws from the seashell fossil: the dry desert was once underwater.

ev.text: "That proves this dry desert once sat beneath a shallow sea."

qs.q: How could Maya tell a fault ran through the canyon wall?
choices: The red stripes on each side of the jagged line did not match.
She found a second seashell fossil resting beside the dark stripe.
The trail markers warned hikers that the river was flooding ahead.
Hot melted rock was still flowing out of the crack near her boots.
qs.why: Paragraph 5 notes that Elena traced a jagged line "where the red stripes no longer lined up."

qs.q: What is this story mostly about?
choices: A sixth-grader collects rare seashells to take back to her science teacher.
A geologist warns her niece about the real dangers of hiking in desert heat.
A girl learns how canyon rocks record millions of years of Earth forces.
An aunt and niece map every dark stripe found inside Red Cedar Canyon.
qs.why: On their hike, Maya discovers how rivers, pressure, ancient seas, molten rock, and tectonic faults shaped the cliffs.

clues.text: piling up hundreds of feet thick
melted deep underground by intense heat
a deep break in Earth's crust where huge blocks of rock shifted past each other

reading.retellFrame: As Maya hikes the canyon with Aunt Elena, she learns that ___ and ___ leave lasting clues in rock.

needsReview.reason: Fictional hike in Red Cedar Canyon illustrating standard geology concepts (sedimentary compaction, marine fossils, igneous dikes, faults, and tectonic plate collisions).
